data.title: Responsive Design
data.tagline: Responsive design is the practice of adapting one interface's layout and interaction to available space and device capabilities.
data.learningOutcome: You can state a layout goal at a specific screen width and verify reading, tapping, and overflow at both desktop and mobile widths.
data.description: At 1440px, a site may show three card columns and full navigation; at 390px, it can use one column, larger touch targets, and collapsed secondary navigation. Breakpoints and media queries are common tools. The goal is not proportional desktop shrinkage but readable, tappable, completable tasks.

learning.assumes: You have opened the same site on a phone and a computer.
learning.outcome: You can state a layout goal at a specific screen width and verify reading, tapping, and overflow at both desktop and mobile widths.

explanation.title: Start with space and interaction
explanation.text: A narrow screen is not merely smaller: line length, touch targets, sidebars, and tables may need reflow. Keep the information and actions required for the current task first.

explanation.title: Rules switch the layout
explanation.text: A breakpoint is a threshold for switching rules, and a media query is CSS syntax for expressing the condition. For example, paste this into project CSS: `@media (max-width: 720px) { .cards { grid-template-columns: 1fr; } }`.

explanation.title: Use browser to simulate mobile views
explanation.text: You don't need a real phone to check mobile layout. In Chrome DevTools, press Cmd+Shift+M (Mac) or Ctrl+Shift+M (Windows) to toggle device simulation. You can select common phone sizes like iPhone 14 or Samsung Galaxy. This is the most important verification step after any layout change - always check both desktop and mobile views before telling the AI you're satisfied. Additionally, Tailwind CSS uses responsive prefixes like sm:, md:, lg: to apply styles at different screen widths, so when AI writes md:grid-cols-3, it means 'use 3 columns from medium screens and up'.

data.boundary: Responsive design is neither identical to media queries nor a separate page only for phones. Media queries are one common tool; the test for responsiveness is whether content and actions remain usable in different spaces.

lessonPractice.title: Three desktop product-card columns make text cramped and buttons too small at 390px. What change should be proposed first?

options.label: Use one or fewer columns at mobile width and check that title, price, and button remain readable and tappable
options.feedback: Correct. Responsive work preserves the ability to complete the current task before preserving every desktop arrangement.

options.label: Scale down the entire desktop page proportionally; three columns must stay unchanged
options.feedback: Scaling makes text and touch targets unusable and does not ensure a mobile task can be completed.

options.label: Hide the title and purchase button, leaving only images to avoid crowding
options.feedback: That removes information and actions needed to buy rather than reorganizing the layout.

data.agentPrompt: In the project CSS, add `@media (max-width: 720px)` for the card area: use one column on mobile while keeping the existing three columns on desktop. Check 390px and 1440px afterward and confirm titles, prices, buttons, and long text are not cramped or horizontally overflowing.
